items.prompt: What does the "mean" of a set of values represent?
choices: The average — the single number that best summarizes where the data is centered
The largest value in the set
The number of values in the set
The difference between the largest and smallest value
items.explanation: Mean is the arithmetic average — a measure of central tendency, not a count, range, or extreme value.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, the new button's conversion rate is described as 18%. What is this 18% an example of?
choices: A mean — the average conversion outcome (0 or 1 per visitor) across the 100 visitors in that group
A confidence interval
A standard deviation
A p-value
items.explanation: A conversion rate is the average of a 0/1 outcome across visitors — mechanically, it's a mean, even though it's usually described as a "rate" or "percentage."

items.prompt: What does "noise" mean in the context of a measured difference?
choices: Random variation that exists in a sample even when there's no true underlying difference
An error in the code that computed the measurement
A difference that's too small to matter for the business
A measurement taken with unreliable instruments
items.explanation: Noise is inherent random sampling variation, not a computational error or a judgment about business importance — it exists even in a perfectly correct measurement.

items.prompt: Two runs of 100 fair-coin flips give 47 heads and 54 heads. Does this gap mean the coin's fairness changed between runs?
choices: No — this gap is exactly the kind of random variation (noise) that occurs even with a genuinely unchanged, fair coin
Yes — any difference between two runs proves the underlying probability changed
No, but only because both counts are close to 50
Yes, but only if the gap is larger than 10
items.explanation: Random sampling naturally produces different-looking results from an unchanged process — the gap by itself is not evidence that anything about the coin changed.

items.prompt: What is a "confidence interval"?
choices: A range around a measured value that's likely to contain the true value, given the sample size and variability observed
The exact, guaranteed true value of a measurement
The number of samples collected
A synonym for the mean of a data set
items.explanation: A confidence interval expresses a plausible range for the true value, not a single guaranteed number — its width reflects how much uncertainty the sample actually supports.

items.prompt: Does a wider confidence interval mean less data was collected, or more?
choices: Less — smaller samples produce wider intervals because there's more uncertainty about where the true value actually is
More — larger samples always produce wider intervals
Interval width has no relationship to sample size
A wider interval always means the measurement was done incorrectly
items.explanation: Smaller samples leave more uncertainty about the true underlying value, which is exactly what a wider confidence interval reflects.

items.prompt: What does "statistically significant" mean, in the specific technical sense this unit uses?
choices: The observed difference is unlikely enough to have come from random noise alone that it's reasonable to treat it as a real effect
The difference is large enough to be commercially important
The difference was measured using an expensive or sophisticated tool
The difference was reviewed and approved by a statistician
items.explanation: Significance is a specific, checkable claim about the chance of noise producing the observed result — not a claim about size, cost, or approval.

items.prompt: Can a small, practically minor difference be "statistically significant"?
choices: Yes — with enough data, even a tiny difference can be unlikely to be pure noise, making it significant despite being practically unimportant
No — significance always implies the difference is large and important
No — only differences above 10% can ever be significant
Yes, but only if the sample size is smaller than 100
items.explanation: Significance and practical importance are separate questions — a large enough sample can make even a small effect statistically significant.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, the team wants to ship based on 18% vs. 12% from 100 visitors per group. What question does this unit say they should ask first?
choices: Could a gap this size arise from random noise alone, given how few visitors were in each group?
Is 18% a bigger number than 12%?
Did the new button cost more to design than the old one?
Would a different button color have converted even higher?
items.explanation: The relevant question isn't whether one number is bigger, but whether the gap is large enough, relative to the sample size, to rule out noise as the explanation.

items.prompt: Why might a 50% relative lift (12% to 18%) be less trustworthy than it sounds, based purely on the Scenario's facts?
choices: Because it was measured from only 100 visitors per group, leaving a lot of room for the gap to be explained by random sampling variation alone
Because 50% relative lifts are mathematically impossible to measure accurately
Because the new button's color was chosen without any design process
Because relative lift can never be trusted, regardless of sample size
items.explanation: The size of the relative lift alone doesn't establish trustworthiness — the sample size behind it determines how much of that lift could plausibly be noise.

items.prompt: Per L2's coin-flip example, why do two runs of 100 flips from the same fair coin give different results?
choices: Each run is a sample, and samples vary by chance even when the underlying process (the coin's true 50% rate) never changes
Because the coin actually becomes less fair after each use
Because 100 flips is too few flips to register any result at all
Because the person doing the flipping influences the outcome
items.explanation: Sampling variation is inherent to any process observed through a finite sample — it doesn't imply the underlying process itself changed.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, how does sample size affect the width of a confidence interval around a measured 12% rate?
choices: A sample of 10,000 produces a much narrower interval than a sample of 100, because more data pins the true rate down more tightly
Sample size has no effect on interval width — only the observed rate itself matters
A larger sample always produces a wider interval, since there's more data to account for
Interval width depends only on which day of the week the data was collected
items.explanation: More data reduces uncertainty about the true rate, which directly narrows the confidence interval — this is exactly why L2's 10,000-visitor row has a much tighter range than the 100-visitor row.

items.prompt: Per L2, is a bigger observed difference always more trustworthy than a smaller one?
choices: Not by itself — trustworthiness depends on the combination of the difference's size and the amount of data behind it
Yes — bigger differences are always more trustworthy regardless of sample size
No — smaller differences are always more trustworthy than bigger ones
Trustworthiness depends only on how the data was visualized
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns against judging trustworthiness by size alone — a large difference from a small sample can be less trustworthy than a small difference from a large sample.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's wrong with treating "significant" as meaning "looks like a big difference"?
choices: Significance is a specific, checkable claim about the chance of noise producing the result — not a subjective impression of how large the difference appears
Nothing — "significant" and "looks big" are interchangeable terms in statistics
It's wrong only when the sample size is under 50
It's wrong only in A/B testing contexts, not in other statistical contexts
items.explanation: L2 frames significance as a precise, computable claim tied to sample size and noise — treating it as a vibe about size misses what the term actually asserts.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, does a wide confidence interval indicate a mistake in how the measurement was computed?
choices: No — a wide interval is the data honestly reporting how little it actually knows yet, given the sample size
Yes — a wide interval always means the formula was applied incorrectly
Yes, but only if the interval is wider than 50 percentage points
No, but only for confidence intervals computed from more than 1,000 data points
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames a wide interval as an honest reflection of limited data, not a computational error — the fix is more data, not re-checking the math.

items.prompt: What's the right response to seeing an unexpectedly wide confidence interval on a measurement?
choices: Recognize that the current sample size doesn't yet support a tight estimate, and consider whether more data is needed before acting on the result
Immediately assume the code that computed it has a bug
Ignore the interval and just use the point estimate as if it were exact
Narrow the interval manually by rounding it to fewer decimal places
items.explanation: A wide interval is information about the current data's limits, not a bug to fix or a detail to ignore — it should inform whether the sample is large enough to act on.

items.prompt: Implement mean, variance, and stdDev for an array of numbers. variance should use the sample variance formula (divide by n - 1).
items.explanation: Variance averages the squared distance of every value from the mean (dividing by n - 1 for a sample); stdDev takes the square root to bring the spread back into the original units, which is what makes it directly interpretable.
items.reference:
📏 Mean — where the data is centered
📐 Variance — average squared spread around the mean
📊 Std. deviation — variance's square root, back in the original units

Why: these three numbers are the building blocks every confidence interval and significance test in this unit is computed from.

items.prompt: Implement twoProportionZTest so it correctly computes the pooled proportion, standard error, z-score, and whether the result is significant at the 95% threshold (|z| >= 1.96).

tests.description: the Scenario's 12/100 vs 18/100 is NOT significant (z well under 1.96)
the same 12%/18% gap from 120/1000 vs 180/1000 IS significant
z is computed correctly (rounded) for the Scenario's numbers

items.explanation: z measures how many standard errors apart the two observed rates are, assuming they actually share one true rate (the pooled proportion) — at only 100 visitors per group the Scenario's z stays under the 1.96 threshold, but the identical 12%/18% gap becomes significant once there's ten times as much data behind it.
items.reference:
🎲 Same effect size, small sample — z stays below 1.96, not significant
📈 Same effect size, larger sample — z clears 1.96, significant

Why: whether a difference counts as significant depends on the sample size behind it, not just how big the gap looks.

items.prompt: Implement twoProportionZTest so it correctly computes the pooled proportion, standard error, z-score, and whether the result is significant at the 95% threshold (|z| >= 1.96).

tests.description: a tiny gap (50/1000 vs 52/1000) is NOT significant
the Scenario's 12/100 vs 18/100 is NOT significant
p1 and p2 are computed as plain proportions

items.explanation: Same test regardless of the specific numbers: z measures how many standard errors separate the two observed rates under the assumption they share one true rate, and a tiny gap needs a very large sample before it can clear the 1.96 threshold.

📈 Same effect size, larger sample — z clears 1.96, significant
